title: Airworthiness Directives; Airbus SAS Airplanes
summary:
The Federal Aviation Administration just issued a new safety rule for certain Airbus A330 passenger and cargo models to fix reports of engine power swinging up and down during descent when the auto-throttle is engaged. Airlines must update computer wiring and settings to turn on a specific engine control feature that keeps power steady, helping prevent unstable approaches.

The people who benefit most are passengers and flight crews, because smoother, more predictable thrust settings reduce the chance of a rushed or unstable approach and an unnecessary go‑around. Pilots get a more consistent descent profile, which can lower workload at a busy phase of flight. Regulators also gain by aligning U.S. action with Europe’s earlier directive and closing a known risk quickly.

Airlines and maintenance providers will bear the immediate impact. The update is relatively simple—mainly labor to change wiring and verify continuity—with the Federal Aviation Administration estimating about $170 per aircraft and no parts cost, affecting 144 U.S. airplanes. Still, there may be short, planned downtimes and scheduling adjustments, and operators will need to incorporate new instructions into their maintenance programs. Smaller operators with tight fleets could feel this more, even if the cost is modest.

The agency made the rule effective October 30, 2025, without the usual advance comment period, citing safety concerns, but it is still taking comments through December 1, 2025. It labels the action as interim, leaving the door open for further steps if new information comes in. Overall, this is a targeted, low-cost fix aimed at improving descent stability and keeping everyday operations safer and more predictable.
